title: Martin Short's Triple-Threat Emmy Season: Home Movies, Grief, and a Little Bit of Betamax
summary:
Martin Short is having an unprecedented (never happened before) Emmy season, and he knows it. The comedian's name is plastered all over this year's nominations, thanks to three wildly different projects. As an actor, he's up for outstanding comedy lead in Hulu's 'Only Murders in the Building' (and he also snagged a comedy series nom as an executive producer). As a game show host, he landed a nod for ABC's 'Match Game.' And then there's the Netflix documentary 'Marty, Life Is Short,' directed by Lawrence Kasdan, which scored three nominations of its own. Short isn't part of the production team on that doc, so he won't personally win if it takes home the prize—but he gave it his full blessing.

How did Kasdan convince the notoriously private Canadian to open up? It took an eight-minute voicemail. Short recalls, '[Kasdan] phoned and said that he and Ron Howard and Imagine would love to do this documentary on me, and I kind of went, "I don't know, I've written a book, I'm Canadian, we're a little more reserved, let me think about it."' Kasdan's epic message explained why Short's story—about celebrating life and using humor to work through grief—was crucial to share. Short also had a goldmine of material: decades of home movies. 'Through all these years, I've always had a camcorder,' he says. 'With all my kids, I would just film.' He handed over shelves of DVDs, and even Steven Spielberg contributed home movies he'd shot with Short. 'So Larry had a great little treasure trove of stuff,' Short says.

The documentary took on deeper meaning when Short's daughter Katherine died in February. Kasdan offered to delay the release, but Short insisted on proceeding. 'We met at his home a few weeks after, and he said, "Netflix will do whatever you want and I will do whatever you want,"' Short says. 'And I thought, this really could be called "Love, Loss and Survival." As I've said in the past, my daughter had mental health struggles. And it's a disease. Some diseases are terminal, whether they're cancer or mental health. And so, I said, "I think we should proceed." And he said, "I think we should too."'

Short's home-video habit actually started thanks to his late friend John Candy, who used Betamax. Short traded in his VHS machine just to swap tapes with him. Now, with three noms, he's heading back to L.A. next month. 'Let's do the cliché, it's a tremendous honor to be recognized by your peers,' he says, then adds with a grin, 'I am Mr. Emmy this year!'
why_it_matters: Short's open discussion of his daughter's death and mental health struggles gives teens a real example of how grief and comedy can exist together, and how being recognized for different kinds of work is possible. It also shows that entertainment awards are not just about acting — they honor producing, hosting, and the personal stories people choose to share.

background_read: Martin Short is a Canadian comedian and actor who became famous on the sketch show SCTV and in movies like Three Amigos and Father of the Bride; today he plays Oliver Putnam in Hulu's Only Murders in the Building (Hulu is a streaming service owned by Disney).
The Emmy Awards are the major U.S. television prizes, and getting nominated for three different jobs in one season is rare, which is why Short's triple-nomination story made news.

The documentary Marty, Life Is Short was directed by Lawrence Kasdan, a veteran filmmaker and screenwriter known for The Big Chill and for writing The Empire Strikes Back, and it includes home movies shot by Steven Spielberg, the director of Jaws, E.T., and Jurassic Park.
The project ties to an older entertainment tradition: John Candy, Short's late friend and fellow comedian, used Betamax tape, so Short traded in his VHS machine to swap home videos with him.

Short also chose to release the film after his daughter died, using his story to talk about mental health struggles and grief, which gives the documentary a much more serious layer than the Emmy comedy nominations suggest.

perspectives.description: Fans of Martin Short see this as a well-earned moment for a comedian who has worked for decades. The documentary also lets audiences connect with him on a human level, because he turned private grief into something public and helpful.

Some could argue that award shows too often celebrate celebrity nostalgia, and that a documentary built on home movies risks feeling self-indulgent. Short himself jokes about the cliché of saying it's an honor, which shows he knows how easily this can look like back-patting.

The three nominations reflect how fragmented television now is: a streamer, a broadcast network, a game show, and a documentary can all compete for the same awards. It also shows how personal archives, home movies, and old formats like Betamax have become raw material for documentary storytelling.

The bigger question is whether this kind of intimate celebrity documentary will lead to more stories about grief and mental health. If it connects with audiences, producers may fund more personal films that mix comedy and loss, rather than only polished celebrity puff pieces.
